Deck overview
What this chapter will establish

A cryptographic claim needs a more precise meaning than “the secret seems safe”. We must say what the attacker receives, what it may do, and what would count as success. The first part of this chapter develops that language; we will then use it to prove security of commitments and pseudorandom functions.

A commitment lets a sender fix a message now and reveal it later. Its two requirements pull in different directions: the published value must conceal the message, but must also prevent the sender from changing it. We will see why satisfying only one requirement is easy, and how Pedersen commitments achieve both under the appropriate assumptions.

‹
Security parameter λ and PPT attackers

A security claim describes a family of systems, indexed by a positive integer , called the security parameter. Increasing makes the security-relevant objects larger. For example, a construction may use random bits or a group whose elements have length proportional to . The parameter is public; hiding its value is not part of security.

PPT stands for probabilistic polynomial time. An attacker is a randomized algorithm whose running time is bounded by a fixed polynomial in its input length, and hence in for the polynomial-size inputs used here. It can perform any computation within that bound and choose later actions from earlier observations. An oracle or protocol definition must separately state which queries and messages it may make.

The notation gives the attacker the security parameter in unary: is a string of ones. This makes “polynomial in input length” agree with “polynomial in the security parameter”. It does not reveal a key.

Computational security quantifies over every such attacker. We cannot prove it by testing a few attack programs. Instead, we bound an arbitrary attacker’s success, usually by showing that a successful attack would solve a problem assumed hard. An asymptotic guarantee still needs concrete parameter choices before it says anything about a particular implementation.

P and NP distinguish deciding from verifying

Many cryptographic statements have an efficiently checkable witness. For example, the public statement may describe a circuit and a required output; a witness gives inputs producing that output. A relation means that the proposed witness passes the prescribed check.

This describes an NP language when is a polynomial and is computable in deterministic polynomial time. A language is a set of yes-instances. The definition says that every yes-instance has a polynomial-size witness that can be checked efficiently. It does not say that we can find that witness efficiently.

P consists of languages whose membership can itself be decided in deterministic polynomial time. Thus . The hypothesis , used in several homework questions, would make efficient witness checking imply efficient decision. Witness search can then be recovered by repeatedly asking whether a partial witness has a valid completion.

NP stands for nondeterministic polynomial time, not “not polynomial”. Exhibiting an exponential exhaustive search does not prove that an NP problem has no better algorithm.

Practice · P versus NP

A Boolean formula has variables. Someone hands you a proposed assignment of 0/1 values. Explain how checking the assignment can be efficient even if finding a satisfying assignment by testing possibilities takes tries. Does this alone prove ?

Reveal step-by-step solution
  1. A witness is the list of proposed truth values.
  2. Evaluate every gate or clause of the formula using those values. The number of operations is polynomial in the formula's written size.
  3. Exhaustive search instead tries up to assignments because each variable has two choices.
  4. This shows an efficient verifier and one potentially expensive search algorithm. It does not show that no clever polynomial-time search algorithm exists. Therefore it does not prove .
Negligible means smaller than every inverse polynomial

Computational security permits a small chance of failure. The important requirement is how that chance changes as grows. A function is negligible if

Read the quantifiers in order. Someone first chooses any fixed inverse-power threshold, such as . We must then be able to choose a point beyond which our function always lies below that threshold. The threshold may be arbitrarily strict, but its exponent stays fixed while grows.

This is stronger than tending to zero. For example, tends to zero but never falls below once . In contrast, eventually falls below every inverse fixed power because exponential growth outpaces every fixed polynomial.

“Non-negligible” is the negation of this definition: for some fixed , the probability is at least at infinitely many security parameters. It need not be large at every parameter. This distinction matters when a theorem rules out every PPT attacker with a non-negligible success probability.

Why polynomially many attempts can remain safe

Suppose a security proof bounds each attempted guess by , and the attacker makes at most attempts. If the bound applies to the relevant events, the union bound gives a total failure probability of at most .

To check negligibility, choose any . The required inequality is

The right-hand inequality eventually holds for every fixed . Therefore polynomially many opportunities do not destroy the negligible bound. The same reasoning handles birthday bounds such as .

This is why security definitions combine polynomial-time attackers with negligible failure. The two conditions are designed to remain useful when an efficient attacker repeats an experiment. The plot lets you compare a candidate function with a chosen threshold; the argument above explains the claim for all sufficiently large parameters.

Computational indistinguishability: the exact definition

Let and be families of distributions, called ensembles. For a fixed security parameter, a distinguisher receives one sample drawn from either or , together with , and outputs a bit. Its algorithm is the same in both experiments.

Each probability includes both the sampling of the input and the distinguisher’s own random choices. The output 1 is simply a decision label. We compare how often the same test uses that label under the two input distributions.

We write , meaning computational indistinguishability, precisely when

This says that every efficient randomized test has negligible advantage. The bound may depend on the test. We do not demand identical distributions or identical samples. We demand that no allowed computation extracts a reliably different signal from them. The base definition supplies a sample; additional oracle access must be included explicitly in the experiment.

If those probabilities are 0.7 and 0.3, the advantage in this convention is 0.4. In an equally likely hidden-world guessing game, the corresponding optimally oriented success probability is . Some texts call the excess over the advantage; that convention differs by a factor of two.

Practice · Distinguishing advantage

An adversary outputs 1 with probability in world and in world . Calculate its distinguishing advantage. Then explain why a constant advantage would contradict computational indistinguishability as grows.

Reveal step-by-step solution
  1. The advantage is .
  2. The value does not shrink as increases, so it cannot be negligible.
  3. If an efficient adversary achieves this constant advantage for arbitrarily large , the two distribution families are not computationally indistinguishable.
  4. This is a probability statement about distinguishability, not about the two individual samples looking similar by eye.
Statistical distance removes the computational restriction

A distribution can conceal information because the information is absent, or because extracting it is computationally difficult. To express the first possibility, compare the distributions directly. For finite distributions on the same set , their statistical distance is

The second expression has a useful interpretation. An unrestricted distinguisher can choose any set , then answer 1 exactly when the sample lies in it. Statistical distance is the largest advantage any such test can achieve, regardless of the cost of deciding membership in .

For Bernoulli distributions with probabilities 0.6 and 0.4 of output 1, the distance is 0.2. Choosing achieves that gap. We call ensembles statistically indistinguishable, written , when is negligible. Distance zero gives perfect indistinguishability.

Statistical indistinguishability implies computational indistinguishability: restricting the available tests cannot increase their maximum advantage. The converse need not hold, because the best statistical test might be computationally infeasible.

What a computational security claim does—and does not—promise

“Computationally secure” means secure against every PPT attacker in the specified experiment, with only negligible failure or distinguishing advantage. The experiment is part of the claim. For message privacy, the attacker tries to distinguish messages; for binding, it tries to produce two inconsistent valid openings.

An unlimited attacker may succeed even when every efficient attacker fails. For example, a deterministic function might turn a uniform λ-bit input into a 2λ-bit output. Its outputs occupy at most 2λ of the 22λ possible strings, so an unlimited observer could enumerate that small output set. Computational indistinguishability would require that no PPT observer can efficiently exploit this difference; the size count alone neither proves nor disproves that requirement.

An information-theoretic guarantee removes the computational restriction. A perfect guarantee allows no relevant gap at all; a statistical guarantee permits a negligible one. The observation model still matters: unlimited computation does not grant secret keys or observations that the experiment withholds.

We will state hiding and binding separately for each commitment scheme. One can be perfect while the other relies on a computational assumption. Calling the entire scheme “secure” without naming those two guarantees conceals the distinction the homework asks you to analyse.

A commitment must hide a choice and prevent changing it

Suppose two participants must choose messages before learning each other’s choice. The first sender cannot reveal its message immediately, because the other participant could then adapt its own choice. Sending a hidden representation is useful only if the sender also cannot revise it later.

The lecture’s rock–paper–scissors example makes both attacks concrete. Sending fails to hide one of three possible moves: the receiver can hash all three and compare. Encrypting the move can hide it, but encryption alone does not guarantee that a later opening fixes a unique move.

For example, with a one-time pad over , send and later reveal . After seeing the other choice, the sender can instead claim any and reveal . The receiver still obtains , so the check cannot detect the change.

A commitment scheme addresses both problems: hiding protects the message from the receiver before opening, and binding prevents the sender from producing inconsistent openings. Neither property follows from the other.

Commit, open, and state the two security requirements

For the non-interactive schemes in this chapter, a public algorithm maps a message and randomizer to a commitment : . The semicolon distinguishes the chosen message from the algorithm’s random input. Parameters and spaces may depend on .

Statistical hiding requires the distributions and to be negligibly close for any allowed candidate messages, with freshly uniform. Perfect hiding makes them identical. Computational hiding instead requires computational indistinguishability.

Computational binding requires that every PPT attacker has negligible probability of outputting such that

The attacker chooses both openings. The success probability includes setup randomness, if present, and the attacker’s coins. Statistical binding removes its computation limit; perfect binding rules out two valid distinct-message openings altogether.

Why hiding and binding require different kinds of security

Perfect hiding says that the receiver sees the same commitment distribution for every message. Fix two messages and a commitment value that occurs with positive probability for . It must also occur for , so both messages have some valid randomizer opening to .

Those openings exist even if nobody can efficiently find both. An unlimited sender can search the finite randomizer spaces until it obtains them. Thus perfect hiding is incompatible with perfect binding in this nontrivial setting.

The same tension persists with negligible statistical errors: almost all mass of the two hiding distributions overlaps, providing openings to both messages that an unbounded search can find. A construction must therefore restrict computation on at least one side. Pedersen uses perfect hiding and computational binding; later examples show the opposite tradeoff.

This explains why the existence of alternative openings is not by itself a break of computational binding. A break must be an efficient method of finding them with non-negligible probability.

HW1 · Problem 2(b)

For each of the following commitment schemes, argue whether it is statistically hiding, statistically binding, both, or neither.

(b) defined as .

Reveal step-by-step solution

Perfectly hiding, but not binding.

  1. Write c = m ⊕ r. The published value is c; the message is m; r is a uniformly chosen bit-string randomizer. XOR is applied at each bit position.

  2. For a small example, publish c = 1001. The message m = 0011 works with r = 1010, because 0011 ⊕ 1010 = 1001.

  3. For hiding, fix any proposed message m and any output c. Exactly one randomizer gives that output: r = c ⊕ m. Since every λ-bit randomizer is equally likely, every c has probability 1/2λ, whatever m is. The receiver sees the same distribution for every message.

  4. Now test binding separately. Keep c = 1001 but change the message to m′ = 1100. Choose r′ = 0101. The new pair still gives 1001. In general choose r′ = c ⊕ m′.

  5. Both different messages pass the opening check. The sender can compute this change efficiently, so even computational binding fails. Perfect hiding did not imply binding.

A randomizer repairs the small-message hash attack

To commit to a short message, choose a secret uniform -bit randomizer and publish

The symbol denotes an unambiguous concatenation. Even if the message has only a few possible values, the receiver cannot test one candidate merely by hashing it: the correct hash input also contains the unknown . Opening reveals , allowing the receiver to recompute the hash.

We still need to justify two claims. For hiding, why do the hash output and the attacker’s queries fail to reveal the message? For binding, why can the sender not find two different message–randomizer pairs with the same hash?

Collision resistance addresses the second question but does not settle the first. A function can reveal a message bit while retaining collision resistance in another part of its output. The next card introduces the stronger ideal model under which we can prove both claims.

A random oracle is a fixed random function accessed by queries

In the random-oracle model, behaves as a uniformly sampled function. Each distinct input receives an independent uniform output; every repetition of an input receives its previous output. Both honest parties and the adversary can query this same function.

A proof need not store the enormous complete table in advance. It can use lazy sampling: store only the input–output pairs that have actually been requested. This produces exactly the same distribution for every possible sequence of queries, including adaptively chosen queries.

A concrete hash such as SHA-3 is a fixed algorithm, not an independently sampled table entry for every possible input. A random-oracle proof therefore establishes security in an ideal model. Replacing the oracle by a real hash is a separate modelling step, not a consequence of collision resistance alone.

Hiding follows until the attacker queries the hidden input

Consider the published value with a uniform -bit . Imagine a comparison experiment in which is sampled independently. Until the attacker asks for the particular input , the oracle’s other replies have the same distribution in both experiments.

This is the useful event to analyse: has the attacker queried the hidden input? Before that happens, the answers supply no information about the remaining randomizer candidates. With at most distinct guesses, the probability of finding a uniform hidden randomizer is at most

The counting uses the whole search, so it remains valid when a new guess depends on earlier failed guesses. We do not assume that its conditional success probability remains after failures.

The real and comparison experiments can differ only on this event. Each candidate-message experiment is therefore close to the independent one; a triangle inequality gives at most twice this bound when comparing two messages. Since a PPT attacker makes polynomially many queries, either bound is negligible. That is the computational-hiding argument.

Practice · Random-oracle guessing bound

In , the randomizer is uniform over . An attacker makes at most random-oracle queries. Bound the probability that it queries the hidden input , and explain why the bound is negligible when is polynomial.

Reveal step-by-step solution

  1. Before the hidden input is queried, the oracle replies do not identify the remaining randomizer. The search therefore has at most opportunities to locate one uniformly hidden value among candidates. Queries with a wrong message or a repeated randomizer cannot increase that coverage. Thus

  2. Because is polynomial, there is a fixed for which for all sufficiently large . To prove negligibility, choose any constant . We need the bound to become smaller than .

  3. The exponential eventually exceeds this fixed polynomial. Since the argument works for every , the hit probability is negligible. This is the event used by the hiding proof: until it occurs, the commitment can be replaced by an independent random output without changing what the attacker observes.

Binding reduces to finding a random-oracle collision

Two accepted openings with different messages give distinct encoded inputs and with . Thus a binding attack provides a collision in the oracle.

If the oracle output has bits, the output at a fresh input is uniform even after all earlier answers are known. Among distinct queried inputs there are pairs. Each pair collides with probability , so

If the attacker outputs openings it never queried, include their two inputs as additional oracle queries before applying the bound. This accounts for all ways its final check can succeed.

The bound becomes substantial around , which is the birthday effect. That is faster than guessing one specified hidden input, but still exponential in . Polynomially many queries give negligible binding failure. The result remains a theorem about the random-oracle model.

HW1 · Problem 1(a)

For each of the following statements, say whether it is TRUE or FALSE. Write at most one sentence to justify your answer.

(a) In the Random Oracle Model, we can build a commitment scheme such that recovering the committed message, or breaking binding (both with non-negligible probability) require that the attacker make an exponential number of oracle queries.

Reveal step-by-step solution

True in the random-oracle model, with sufficiently long randomizers and outputs.

  1. A random oracle assigns independent uniform outputs to distinct inputs and remembers its answers for repeated inputs. Set c = H(m ∥ r), where ∥ joins the message m with a secret fresh randomizer r. Later reveal m and r to open c.

  2. If r contains λ random bits, it has 2λ possibilities. Testing Q distinct candidates covers at most Q of them, giving the hidden-input guessing bound min(1, Q/2λ). For λ = 4 and Q = 2, that is 2/16. These small numbers illustrate the counting, not real security.

  3. For binding, the attacker needs two different message openings with the same output. Among Q queried input pairs there are Q(Q−1)/2 pairs to compare. If each output has λ bits, a particular pair collides with probability 1/2λ. The union bound is therefore at most min(1, Q(Q−1)/(2·2λ)).

  4. The collision bound counts all collisions, including some with the same message, so it is still a valid upper bound for the binding attack.

  5. A constant success chance needs roughly 2λ hidden-input guesses or 2λ/2 collision-search queries. Both are exponential in λ. Hiding here means learning information about the committed message beyond what was already known; if a message is already known, “recovering” it is not a meaningful security test.

HW1 · Problem 1(d)

For each of the following statements, say whether it is TRUE or FALSE. Write at most one sentence to justify your answer.

(d) The commitment scheme is provably secure if is a cryptographic hash function like SHA-3.

Reveal step-by-step solution

False as a claim derived merely from ordinary hash-function security.

  1. First separate the two required properties. Binding stops different openings from passing the same check. Hiding stops the receiver distinguishing which message was committed.

  2. Collision resistance helps binding: two different accepted openings would give two different hash inputs with the same output.

  3. It does not by itself guarantee hiding. Imagine defining a function whose output contains the first bit of the message, followed by a collision-resistant digest of the full input. Finding a collision in this new function would still require a collision in the digest component.

  4. Nevertheless its first output bit openly reveals the first message bit. This is enough to disprove hiding, even if the rest of the digest is hard to attack.

  5. The ideal random-oracle proof uses stronger behavior than collision resistance. This argument does not demonstrate an attack on SHA-3; it explains why the stated assumption alone is not a proof of this commitment’s security.

Division in the exponent uses a finite field

Cryptographic equations often use exponents in , with arithmetic modulo a prime . This set is a field: every nonzero element has a multiplicative inverse. Consequently we can solve a linear equation by division, provided the divisor is nonzero modulo .

For example, in . Since , multiplying by 4 gives . The notation in this field means , not the real number .

Primality matters. Modulo 12, the nonzero value 3 has no inverse, so that division is unavailable. More generally, has an inverse modulo exactly when ; a prime modulus guarantees this for every nonzero residue.

Later, two valid openings or proof responses will give an equation . The crucial proof step will be establishing . Only then can we extract the secret as . We introduce the field here because that justification carries the security argument.

Practice · Modular division

Solve . Show every step and explain why dividing by 3 is valid. Then explain what goes wrong with division by 3 modulo 12.

Reveal step-by-step solution
  1. Compute , so the inverse of 3 modulo 11 is 4.
  2. Multiply both sides by 4: .
  3. Check: .
  4. Modulo 12, no inverse of 3 exists: every multiple of 3 is divisible by 3, so it cannot equal 1 modulo 12.
  5. Therefore modular “division” must be justified by the existence of an inverse, which prime moduli guarantee for nonzero values.
What “a group of prime order q” actually means

A group is a set with an associative operation, an identity element, and an inverse for every element. The operation stays inside . We write it multiplicatively, but its elements need not be ordinary numbers; in other cryptographic settings they can be points on an elliptic curve.

The order of the group is its number of elements. Saying “ has prime order ” means exactly , where is prime. It does not mean that every element is a prime number, or that the operation must reduce modulo .

The group axioms justify cancellation and the usual laws of powers. For example, multiplying by gives . A cyclic group also lets us describe every element as a power of one generator; that is the next link we need.

Generators connect group elements to exponents

A group is cyclic if some element , called a generator, reaches every element through its powers. In a group of order , the values are distinct and . Hence

For our three-element group, gives , , , and , all modulo 7. This is why group elements and exponents have different arithmetic domains.

Every nonidentity element of a prime-order group is a generator. One reason is Lagrange’s theorem: an element’s order divides the group order. When that order is prime, the only choices are 1 for the identity and for every other element. Such a group is therefore cyclic.

Writing tells us that an exponent exists and is unique in . It does not give us an efficient way to recover from the representation of . The gap between existence and efficient recovery is the basis of discrete-logarithm security.

Practice · Work with a prime-order group

Let be the subgroup generated by under multiplication modulo 23. Show that its order is 11 by calculating powers, and explain the difference between this group and .

Reveal step-by-step solution
  1. The powers of 2 modulo 23 are .
  2. The first return to identity 1 occurs at exponent 11, so the subgroup has exactly 11 elements. Its order is the prime .
  3. In , we multiply elements modulo 23. By contrast, the exponents belong to , where we add and multiply integer residues modulo 11.
  4. The rule connects these two structures. Distinguishing the group operation from exponent arithmetic is essential for Pedersen commitments.
The discrete-logarithm assumption is a quantified claim

Consider a family of efficiently described cyclic groups , of prime order , with generator . The group parameters are public. Sample uniformly from and publish . The discrete logarithm problem is to recover from those public values.

The assumption says that for every PPT algorithm , some negligible bounds this probability. It includes the random exponent, the attacker’s randomness, and random group setup when that is part of the family. Group operations and exponentiation by a known exponent must be efficient.

For a tiny group, we can enumerate powers and recover the exponent; our examples deliberately allow that so the equations can be checked. The assumption concerns a suitable growing family of cryptographic groups. Prime order alone does not make discrete logarithms hard.

Pedersen’s binding proof will turn any successful double opening into this exact recovery task. Its hiding proof will not use the assumption.

A reduction turns a hypothetical attack into a solver

To prove “discrete-logarithm hardness implies binding”, assume we have an efficient program that breaks binding. We then construct a program that uses to solve a discrete-logarithm challenge. This construction is a security reduction.

The reduction has two responsibilities. First, it must supply the attacker with the same distribution of inputs and messages as the attack experiment. Otherwise the attacker’s claimed success probability says nothing about this run. Second, it must transform a successful attack into a correct answer to its own challenge.

Practice · A reduction is a logical implication

You want to prove: “If DLP is hard, a commitment scheme is binding.” Write its contrapositive. Explain the inputs and outputs of a reduction algorithm that uses a hypothetical binding attacker .

Reveal step-by-step solution
  1. The desired implication is .
  2. Its contrapositive is .
  3. Assume an efficient outputs two different valid openings of one commitment.
  4. Build : on input DLP instance , give to , collect its two openings, and algebraically derive the hidden exponent such that .
  5. If breaks binding often, solves DLP often. But DLP hardness excludes such an efficient . Therefore binding must hold. The key is constructing the solver, not asserting that the problems seem related.
Pedersen commits with two public generators

Choose a cyclic group of prime order , with public generators . The sender must not know the discrete logarithm satisfying . For message , sample uniform and publish

Opening reveals , and verification recomputes the product. The message and randomizer are field elements used as exponents; the commitment is a group element. Knowing makes the forward computation efficient.

The factor makes the output uniform over the group, concealing the message. At the same time, changing while retaining the same commitment requires compensating in the exponent of . A double opening will reveal the relation between and , which is assumed hard to compute.

The setup condition is therefore substantive. If a party chose and retained , it could adjust openings. A security theorem must account for how the public generators are generated, rather than merely describe them as “random-looking”.

Pedersen’s homomorphism preserves a relation between messages

Suppose and . Multiplying the public commitments gives

The rearrangement is valid because a cyclic group is commutative. All sums in the exponents are modulo . The receiver can compute the left side without learning either message; someone who knows both openings can open the result to their sum.

This is a homomorphic property: a public operation on commitments corresponds to a specified operation on their hidden messages. Raising a commitment to a known scalar similarly produces . Combining these operations supports linear combinations.

The resulting object is still a commitment. The homomorphism does not reveal the sum, and it does not by itself give a way to multiply two unknown messages. Keeping track of the operation supported by the construction prevents that common overextension.

Perfect hiding follows from a uniform group mask

Fix any message . Because is a generator, a uniform makes uniform over . Multiplication by the fixed element is a bijection of the group, so is also uniform. Every commitment occurs with probability , independently of the message.

We can express the same fact in exponents to make the unique opening explicit. There is a nonzero with . For any target , the equation has exactly one solution:

The inverse exists because and is prime. Each target commitment therefore corresponds to exactly one of the equally likely randomizers, whatever is.

This proof may refer to and without computing them. It proves a statement about distributions, not an algorithm for finding an alternative opening. Thus hiding is perfect even for an unlimited receiver, while the difficulty of finding those exponents can still protect binding against efficient senders.

A double Pedersen opening reveals the discrete logarithm

Suppose an attacker outputs distinct messages with valid openings to the same commitment. A reduction receives as its discrete-logarithm challenge and uses those public generators for the attack. Acceptance gives

The implication uses that has order . Rearranging yields . If , this equation would force , contradicting a successful binding attack. Thus the nonzero difference has an inverse, and

If the discrete-logarithm challenge has h = 1, the reduction immediately returns x = 0; otherwise h is a valid generator for the attack. Every successful double opening yields the right logarithm. Apart from efficient checking and field arithmetic, the reduction runs the attacker once. Consequently a non-negligibly successful PPT binding attacker would contradict the discrete-logarithm assumption.

HW1 · Problem 2(a)

For each of the following commitment schemes, argue whether it is statistically hiding, statistically binding, both, or neither.

(a) defined as where is a hash function (modeled as a random oracle) from to a cyclic group of prime order .

Reveal step-by-step solution

Neither statistically hiding nor statistically binding.

  1. The rule is c = H(r)m. Here H(r) is a group element, m is an exponent modulo the group order q, and the identity element is written 1.

  2. Test message m = 0 first. Every group element to exponent zero equals 1. The output is therefore always 1, regardless of r.

  3. For message m = 1, the output is H(r), which is uniform in the group in this model. It equals 1 with probability 1/q. The test “is the output 1?” distinguishes the two messages with probability gap 1−1/q. Hiding fails.

  4. Statistical binding must resist unlimited computation. Query two distinct randomizers r₁,r₂. Choose a generator g and compute exponents a,b such that H(r₁)=ga and H(r₂)=gb. Computing these discrete logarithms is allowed to this unlimited attacker.

  5. If a ≠ b, choose message m₁=b with randomizer r₁, and message m₂=a with randomizer r₂. Both give gab, but the messages differ. That is a double opening.

  6. The independent uniform exponents a,b coincide with probability 1/q, so the attack succeeds with probability 1−1/q. For example, bases g² and g³ open to the same value using messages 3 and 2. This establishes the statistical-binding failure without claiming the discrete logarithms are efficiently computable.

HW1 · Problem 2(c)

For each of the following commitment schemes, argue whether it is statistically hiding, statistically binding, both, or neither.

(c) The Pedersen commitment scheme, when the discrete logarithm such that between the public generators and of is known.

Reveal step-by-step solution

Perfectly hiding, but not binding when the relation between the generators is known.

  1. Write h = gx, with known nonzero x. The commitment becomes c = gmhr = gm+xr. All exponent calculations below are modulo q.

  2. Why hiding remains: multiplication by nonzero x rearranges the q possible remainders because x has an inverse. Adding a fixed m also rearranges them. Therefore uniform r makes m+xr uniform, independently of the chosen message.

  3. To change the message to m′ while keeping c, keep its exponent equal: m+xr ≡ m′+xr′. Subtract m′, then multiply by the inverse of x. This gives r′ = r+(m−m′)x⁻¹ modulo q.

  4. Example: q=11, x=3, m=2, r=3. The exponent is 2+3·3=11, or remainder 0. Since 3·4≡1 modulo 11, x⁻¹=4. Choose m′=7; then r′=3+(2−7)·4≡5. The new exponent 7+3·5=22 also has remainder 0.

  5. Both openings produce the same group element. The arithmetic is efficient when x is known, so binding fails. Real Pedersen setup must keep that relation hard for the sender to find.

HW1 · Problem 2(d)

For each of the following commitment schemes, argue whether it is statistically hiding, statistically binding, both, or neither.

(d) The “ElGamal commitment scheme”, defined as , in the same setting as the Pedersen commitment scheme ( s.t. is known).

Reveal step-by-step solution

Perfectly binding, but not statistically hiding.

  1. Call the published pair (a,b) = (gr, gmhr). Suppose two openings (m,r) and (m′,r′) produce that identical pair.

  2. The first coordinates agree: gr=gr′. Powers of a generator repeat exactly modulo the group order q, so r=r′ as allowed remainders.

  3. Cancel the now-equal mask hr in the second coordinates. We get gm=gm′, hence m=m′ modulo q. Distinct allowed messages cannot open the same pair. This is perfect binding, even against unlimited computation.

  4. For hiding, use the known x with h=gx. Compute b/ax. Since ax=grx=hr, this cancels the mask and leaves gm. Division here uses a group inverse.

  5. An unlimited observer can recover m by a discrete logarithm. Moreover an efficient observer given two candidate messages can compare their powers to gm. Thus the scheme is not statistically hiding; with known x it also fails the usual message-distinguishing version of computational hiding.

A PRF must withstand adaptively chosen oracle queries

A pseudorandom function (PRF) is an efficiently computable keyed function . One uniform secret key is chosen for the whole experiment. The resulting function is deterministic, so repeated inputs have repeated outputs.

Compare two experiments. In the real experiment, an adversary queries . In the random experiment, it queries one uniformly sampled function . The adversary can select inputs adaptively from all previous answers. It does not receive the secret key or a description of the random function.

The superscript denotes oracle access, not exponentiation. The probabilities include the key or random function and the adversary’s coins. PRF security requires this advantage to be negligible for every PPT oracle adversary. This is stronger than saying that one isolated output appears random: it concerns the entire adaptive conversation.

Practice · Repeated PRF queries

An attacker queries a black-box function on input twice and receives . Could this black box be a pseudorandom function or a truly random function as defined in the lecture? Explain the distinction from independent random samples.

Reveal step-by-step solution
  1. Both the keyed PRF and a sampled random function assign one fixed output to each input.
  2. Repeating must therefore return the same in both worlds.
  3. If , the oracle is not behaving like either kind of function.
  4. Independent fresh random samples on every call are a different experiment. Security comparisons must reproduce the complete interface, not just the randomness of individual outputs.
HW1 · Problem 1(b)

For each of the following statements, say whether it is TRUE or FALSE. Write at most one sentence to justify your answer.

(b) If P = NP, then secure PRFs exist.

Reveal step-by-step solution

False: secure PRFs are incompatible with P = NP.

  1. A PRF uses one secret key k to define every answer F(k,x). A genuinely random function instead chooses independent answers at different inputs and remembers them.

  2. Collect answers y₁,…,yₜ at distinct inputs x₁,…,xₜ. Ask the yes/no question: “Does some key k satisfy F(k,xᵢ)=yᵢ for every observed pair?” A proposed key can be checked by evaluating F on the listed inputs. It is an efficiently checkable witness, so this is an NP question.

  3. If P=NP, this existence question can be decided efficiently. No unexplained key-recovery step is needed: the yes/no answer itself will distinguish the experiments.

  4. In the real-PRF experiment the answer is always yes, because the actual key fits. In the random-function experiment, suppose keys have κ bits and outputs have ℓ bits. A fixed key matches t independent random answers with probability 2−ℓt. There are at most 2κ keys, so the union bound gives at most 2κ−ℓt for any key fitting.

  5. Choose polynomially many distinct inputs so ℓt exceeds κ by the desired security margin, as available in the standard PRF setting. Then the random-function experiment almost always answers no, while the PRF experiment always answers yes. An efficient distinguisher contradicts PRF security.

Homomorphic encryption states correctness after decryption

Fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) allows a server to evaluate a circuit on encrypted inputs. The client generates a secret key and any public evaluation material, encrypts a message , and sends its ciphertext . The server uses to obtain an encryption of the circuit’s output without decrypting .

This is the correctness relation, up to the failure probability allowed by the scheme and its parameters. The evaluation key contains public material needed for the supported computation. The ciphertext may be randomized, so correctness does not require equality with the bytes of a fresh encryption of .

For example, evaluating a circuit that maps to should yield a ciphertext decrypting to . There may be many ciphertexts with that same decryption. The homework asks you to distinguish this semantic guarantee from the stronger, generally unjustified claim that two ciphertext representations are identical.

HW1 · Problem 1(c)

For each of the following statements, say whether it is TRUE or FALSE. Write at most one sentence to justify your answer.

(c) In a FHE scheme, given a ciphertext , we have that .

Reveal step-by-step solution

False if the statement requires identical ciphertexts.

  1. Enc(m) means encrypt message m, producing a ciphertext c. Dec(c) means decrypt it. Eval(f,c) computes a new encrypted representation intended to represent f(m).

  2. Encryption normally uses randomness. Two encryptions of the same message can therefore have different bytes while decrypting to the same value.

  3. Write the randomness explicitly: c₁ = Enc(pk,3;r₁) and c₂ = Enc(pk,3;r₂), where pk is the public encryption key. Different random choices r₁ and r₂ may produce c₁ ≠ c₂ while both decrypt to 3.

  4. The correctness requirement is Dec(Eval(f,c)) = f(m), for a valid encryption c of m and functions supported by the scheme. If m=3 and f doubles its input, the evaluated ciphertext must decrypt to 6.

  5. It need not equal a newly sampled Enc(6) byte for byte. The missing distinction in the proposed equality is between the encrypted representation and its decrypted content.

DDH compares a linked exponent with an independent one

In a cyclic group of prime order with generator , sample independent uniform . The decisional Diffie–Hellman (DDH) problem asks us to distinguish these distributions:

The attacker receives the group elements and public parameters, not the displayed exponents. In the real distribution the third exponent is the product of the first two. In the random distribution it is sampled independently. Multiplying the first two group elements only gives , so it does not directly test the required product relation.

The DDH assumption requires a negligible bound for every PPT in the chosen group family; security parameters and group descriptions are implicit in this abbreviated formula. It is a separate assumption from discrete-logarithm hardness. Some groups permit an efficient product-relation test even though recovering exponents remains hard.

Reveal step-by-step solution
  1. In a real triple , so its exponent equals the product of the secret exponents of and modulo .
  2. In a fake triple for a fresh independent uniform .
  3. The attacker sees , not the exponents .
  4. DDH assumes no efficient test has non-negligible distinguishing advantage between these distributions. The relation exists mathematically, but efficiently detecting it from the public group elements is the hard task.
A candidate PRF: hash to a group, then exponentiate

Let be a random oracle into a prime-order group, and choose a uniform secret key . Define

The same key is used for every input. A repeated input gives the same hash and therefore the same function value. The claim is that the function behaves like a random function to an efficient observer with access to both and the function being tested, assuming DDH hardness.

The connection is visible for one input. If , then its real PRF output is . This resembles the linked DDH pair. A reduction must exploit that resemblance while still supplying independent random-oracle values at different inputs.

We first study the lecture’s restricted reduction with one PRF query. The homework then removes the loss from guessing its location and finally handles arbitrary polynomially many PRF queries. Those are different simulation tasks, so we will state the restriction at each step.

Embed a DDH challenge at one oracle input

The reduction receives . Its task is to decide whether or an independent uniform group element. It runs a PRF adversary internally and answers its oracle queries without knowing or .

For the restricted lecture argument, first suppose the adversary’s sole PRF query will be at a designated input . Set . At every other distinct input , sample uniform and store . These values have the required independent uniform distribution, and storing them preserves repeat consistency.

Check both simulated worlds, then account for the guess

In the real DDH case, . Because the reduction set , its response is exactly . The hidden PRF key is , although the reduction never learns it.

In the random DDH case, is an independent uniform group element. Returning it for the one permitted PRF query gives the required random-function response, even when the adversary has already seen the hash answers. Thus a useful distinguishing gap transfers between these two experiments.

The real adversary may choose its PRF input after observing several oracle answers. In the lecture’s restricted setting, that input is among at most distinct hash queries. The reduction guesses one query position uniformly before the run and embeds there. Other hash replies are distributed identically, so the guess is hidden from the adversary.

It succeeds in selecting the later PRF input with probability ; on other runs it aborts with a fixed unbiased output. If has advantage , this gives DDH advantage in the stipulated setting. A polynomial loss still preserves non-negligibility. The following homework improves this construction rather than reusing it outside its one-query restriction.

Practice · Account for reduction loss

A PRF distinguisher has advantage and makes at most random-oracle queries. A DDH reduction guesses which RO input will later be used as the unique PRF query. Explain why the constructed DDH advantage is at least , and which assumption permits a negligible conclusion.

Reveal step-by-step solution
  1. If selects one of the candidate RO positions uniformly, it chooses the correct one with probability .
  2. Conditional on guessing correctly, provides a proper PRF-vs-random simulation, so 's distinguishing behavior gives advantage .
  3. When the guess is wrong, aborts rather than pretending to have a valid simulation.
  4. Combining yields advantage at least (using an unbiased fallback on abort).
  5. If is polynomial and DDH advantage must be negligible, then a non-negligible would contradict DDH hardness. Hence the PRF is secure for the stipulated adversary.
HW1 · Problem 3(a)

Problem 3: A tight proof for our cool PRF. Recall the PRF from the lecture, where is a hash function (modeled as a random oracle) from to a cyclic group of prime order , and .

In class, we showed that for any PPT adversary making at most random oracle queries, and a single PRF query, we can build a DDH adversary such that .

Let’s now strengthen this result. For now, we still consider a PRF adversary that makes a single PRF query. Intuitively, what we want is to embed the DDH challenge into every RO query, so that we don’t have to guess which RO query is for the message that will be used to query the PRF.

(a) Consider the following simulation of by , upon receiving a DDH challenge :

  • On every RO query , sets .
  • Upon receiving the PRF query , returns .
  • outputs whatever outputs.

What can you say about the advantage of ?

Reveal step-by-step solution

The proposed simulation is not the random-oracle experiment, so the claimed advantage transfer is unjustified.

  1. The simulation answers every distinct hash query with the same value X. A true random oracle instead samples an independent uniform group value at each new input, and only repeats an answer when the input repeats.

  2. Ask two different inputs m₁,m₂ and compare the outputs. In the proposed simulation, H(m₁)=H(m₂) with probability 1.

  3. In a random oracle with q possible outputs, the second independent output matches the first with probability 1/q. The gap is 1−1/q, which is easy to detect.

  4. An attacker that works well against the genuine PRF game may behave completely differently on this detectable fake game. Therefore its PRF advantage does not automatically become a DDH advantage.

  5. This does not claim every possible attacker has DDH advantage zero. It says the proposed simulation gives no general justification for the promised reduction. Correct the distribution before using the attacker’s assumed guarantee.

HW1 · Problem 3(b)

(b) Let be an arbitrary DDH triple. Show how to build a new triple such that:

  • is uniformly random in ;
  • if is a “real” DDH triple (i.e., ), then is a “real” DDH triple;
  • if is a “fake” DDH triple (i.e., for a random ), then is a “fake” DDH triple.
Reveal step-by-step solution

Shift both relevant exponents using the same fresh random number.

  1. Let X=gα, Y=gβ, Z=gγ. We do not need to know those exponents to perform the group operations. Pick a uniform r in Z_q, then set X′=Xgr and Z′=ZYr. Keep Y unchanged.

  2. The exponent of X′ is α+r. Adding a fixed value to all possible remainders rearranges them, so uniform r makes X′ uniform.

  3. In the real case γ=αβ. The new third exponent is αβ+βr=(α+r)β. Thus Z′=(X′)β, exactly the real relation for the new first element.

  4. In the random case γ is independent and uniform. Conditional on r, adding βr to γ preserves uniformity. Thus Z′ is uniform and independent of X′ and Y in the random-challenge experiment.

  5. Example in exponent arithmetic modulo 5: α=1, β=2, r=3. Then α′=4 and the real γ′=2+2·3≡3. Also α′β=4·2≡3. This numerical check illustrates the general algebra; it is not a security proof by itself.

HW1 · Problem 3(c)

(c) Use your solution from (b) to build a better simulation of by so that:

(note that we still only consider a PRF adversary that makes a single PRF query).

Reveal step-by-step solution

Use a separate stored shift for each distinct input; one PRF answer then has the exact required distribution.

  1. Maintain a table indexed by the queried message. The first time input mᵢ appears, choose a fresh uniform rᵢ and store H(mᵢ)=Xgrᵢ. If the input repeats, return that stored value. If the PRF input appears first, create its table entry then.

  2. Each fresh shift rearranges all exponents, so each new hash answer is uniform. The shifts are independent, so distinct hash inputs receive independent answers. The table ensures repeated inputs remain consistent.

  3. For the one allowed PRF query mⱼ, return ZYrⱼ. In the real DDH world Z=gαβ, so this equals g(α+rⱼ)β=H(mⱼ)β. It is the genuine PRF with key β.

  4. In the random DDH world, Z is an independent uniform group element. Multiplying it by Yrⱼ keeps this single response uniform even given the hash answers. It therefore matches the one answer of a genuinely random function.

  5. The two distributions match exactly for this single-query setting. The reduction no longer guesses which hash query will later matter, so there is no query-index probability loss. Multiple PRF answers need the separate analysis in the next exercise.

HW1 · Problem 3(d)

(d) [Bonus]: Show how to extend your solution from (c) to handle an arbitrary number of PRF queries.

Hint: Given a DDH challenge , show how to build a new triple as in (b), but with the additional property that when the DDH challenge is fake, the value is uniformly random in and independent of and .

Reveal step-by-step solution

Use two independent random numbers per input so that both output exponents can vary independently.

  1. For each new message mᵢ choose independent uniform uᵢ,vᵢ in Z_q. Store H(mᵢ)=Xuᵢgvᵢ and f(mᵢ)=ZuᵢYvᵢ. Return stored values on repeats. The symbols u and v here name random exponents, not protocol messages.

  2. In the real DDH case, the exponent of the first value is aᵢ=αuᵢ+vᵢ. The second exponent is αβuᵢ+βvᵢ=βaᵢ. Hence every answer satisfies f(mᵢ)=H(mᵢ)β, all under one key β.

  3. In the random case, the exponent pair is aᵢ=αuᵢ+vᵢ and bᵢ=γuᵢ+βvᵢ. The map from (uᵢ,vᵢ) to (aᵢ,bᵢ) has matrix [[α,1],[γ,β]] over Z_q and determinant αβ−γ. A matrix with nonzero determinant over a field is invertible, so every output pair has exactly one input pair.

  4. Therefore independent uniform input pairs give independent uniform output pairs. Fresh uᵢ,vᵢ for distinct messages also make those pairs independent across messages. This is the joint distribution that a random oracle and independent random function require.

  5. The exceptional event γ=αβ occurs with probability 1/q when γ is uniformly random. On that event the output exponents are related, so we cannot claim exact random-world equality. Allowing this event gives advantage loss at most 1/q, rather than a multiplicative loss for guessing one query.

  6. Invertibility is what makes the simulation work: every pair is produced equally often, so the answers have the joint distribution required by the random experiment.

A vector commitment binds values to their positions

A vector commitment binds an ordered list to one public commitment . An opening for index supplies the claimed value and a proof . The verification algorithm checks .

Position binding requires that every PPT attacker has negligible probability of finding one , one valid index , and two distinct messages with accepted openings:

The index is fixed in both claims. Opening different values at different positions is ordinary functionality, not an attack. This homework requires position binding but does not require hiding.

The next constructions compare two costs: the commitment sent once and the extra proof accompanying one opened entry. Publishing all entry hashes gives a long commitment and an empty extra proof. Hashing the entire vector gives a short commitment but a long opening. A Merkle tree will make both costs small.

HW1 · Problem 4(a)

(a) Describe a secure vector commitment scheme where the commitment is of size bits and an opening proof is of size bits. Argue that your scheme is position binding in the RO model.

Reveal step-by-step solution

Publish one hash value per position.

  1. For vector (m₁,…,mₙ), publish c=(H(m₁),…,H(mₙ)). Each hash has λ bits, so n of them use nλ bits. The index determines which coordinate is being claimed.

  2. To open index i, supply the message mᵢ. The verifier computes H(mᵢ) and compares it with the stored coordinate cᵢ. No additional hash path or other proof data is required: the extra proof π is empty.

  3. The problem counts the size of π separately from the claimed index and message. Thus π has constant size O(1); this does not mean communicating the index and the message costs zero bits.

  4. If two different messages both verify at the same index, their hashes both equal cᵢ. They are distinct inputs with the same hash output: a collision. The random-oracle collision bound makes finding this unlikely with polynomially many queries.

  5. Example: publishing eight 256-bit hashes uses 2048 bits. Opening one entry adds no extra authentication hashes, but you still send the entry you want checked.

HW1 · Problem 4(b)

(b) Describe a secure vector commitment scheme where the commitment is of size bits and an opening proof is of size bits, where is the size in bits of a message.

Reveal step-by-step solution

Publish one hash of the complete, unambiguously encoded vector.

  1. Encode the ordered messages so their boundaries are clear, then publish c=H(encode(m₁,…,mₙ)). For fixed-length messages simple concatenation works; for variable lengths include lengths or another unambiguous encoding.

  2. One hash output uses λ bits, whatever the vector length. That makes the commitment short.

  3. To check a particular index, the straightforward verifier needs the full vector. Supply all messages as the opening information, recompute the complete digest, and check both that digest and the claimed index value.

  4. If each message has |m| bits, this opening contains O(n|m|) bits. The claimed value can be omitted from the auxiliary proof if the verifier already receives it separately; the asymptotic bound is unchanged.

  5. If different values at the same index both verify, the two complete encodings differ but have the same hash. That gives a collision. The construction trades a short commitment for a long opening; it does not hide the other messages when opened.

A Merkle opening reveals the missing inputs along one path

A Merkle tree commits to a vector using a root hash. Hash each entry to obtain its leaf value, then hash ordered pairs of children until one root remains. Fix the tree shape and distinguish leaf encodings from internal-node encodings so the verifier interprets every hash input unambiguously.

To authenticate one entry, the verifier starts from its leaf hash. It cannot compute the parent without the sibling hash. Once that sibling is supplied, it can compute the parent, which becomes the known child at the next level. Supplying one sibling at each level is therefore enough to reconstruct the root.

A balanced tree has levels, so the sibling hashes use bits. This cost follows from what verification needs at each step; the root does not contain a recoverable copy of every entry.

HW1 · Problem 4(c)

(c) Describe a secure vector commitment scheme where the commitment is of size bits and an opening proof is of size bits. Hint: Build a tree!

Reveal step-by-step solution

Use a balanced binary Merkle tree and reveal one sibling hash per level.

  1. Hash each message to form a leaf. Hash every ordered pair of neighboring child hashes to form a parent. Continue until the root, and publish that one λ-bit value. Fix the tree shape, index range and leaf/internal-node encoding so verification is unambiguous.

  2. To open one leaf, the verifier starts with the hash of the claimed message. At each level it needs the other child’s hash: the sibling. The index tells whether the current value belongs on the left or right.

  3. For leaf 4 of 8, first combine leaf hash 3 on the left with leaf hash 4 on the right. Then combine the hash of leaves 1–2 on the left. Finally combine the hash of leaves 5–8 on the right. These three sibling values rebuild the root.

  4. A balanced tree of n leaves has O(log₂ n) levels, so the proof has O(log n · λ) bits of sibling hashes, plus any needed index/shape information. For n=8 the sibling portion is exactly three hash values.

  5. For binding, compare two accepted openings for different messages at the same index. If their initial leaf hashes already agree, they give a collision. Otherwise trace upward: the roots agree, so there is a first point where different child inputs give the same parent hash. That too is a collision.

  6. This gives both a short commitment and a short opening. Left/right order is essential: the same hashes in the wrong order need not reconstruct the root.
